detail.abstract:
Big Tech’s unchecked power has evolved from a regulatory crisis into one concerning the rule of law itself. Shielded by the First Amendment, Section 230 of the 1996 Communications Decency Act, corporate law, and contract law, technology giants have circumvented traditional government oversight, amassing a level of power that eclipses even that of some sovereign states. No longer guided by cautious boards of directors, today’s tech empires are often ruled by impulsive billionaire CEOs, who, through a single policy change or algorithmic tweak, can upend individual rights, destabilize global markets, and erode democratic governance itself.

The scale of such dangers escalates as tech oligarchs inch closer to the levers of government power—occupying advisory roles, funding political campaigns, and, in some cases, directing state policy itself. What was once a culture of innovation—”moving fast and breaking things”—has metastasized into corporate vigilantism. Major platforms and their oligarchs have effectively privatized a pseudo-sovereign bundle of rights, a set of enforcement powers that range from digital dispossessions to cyber countermeasures and algorithmic bans. A rogue corporate leader, invoking the rhetoric of cybersecurity, platform integrity, or foreign cyber interference, can now leverage the unprecedented power of modern tech giants with few legal restraints.

Yet the legal system already possesses the tools to rein in this unchecked power. Private law, long used to set the lawful boundaries of individual self-help, offers a doctrinal basis to distinguish between legitimate acts of corporate discretion and unlawful corporate vigilantism. This Article argues for reviving private law principles to impose meaningful constraints on tech companies’ growing pseudo sovereign authority. Only by reaffirming the doctrinal boundaries that have historically constrained private unilateral discretion can courts, legislatures, and even corporate actors themselves restore the balance between innovation, autonomy, and public accountability. If left unaddressed, the unfettered expansion of corporate vigilantism will not only entrench Big Tech’s market dominance but also erode the foundational legal principles that separate private enterprise from state power.

detail.abstract: Kalshi markets its daily rain contract to small businesses as a weather hedge. I test this claim on New York rooftop bars, the case where it should work best, using 355 season days of settlement data, hourly Central Park rainfall and reconstructed profiles of ten venues, with the core definitions time-stamped before data collection. The contract is well calibrated (Brier score 0.143, against 0.146 for the National Weather Service) but pays on the wrong index: 69% of payouts (95% CI 62-75) fall on evenings that were not lost, and the buyer pays $2.75 of premium per dollar of useful payout. Hedging gains are small and disappear under realistic execution, and a better-informed buyer does not fix the problem. A counterfactual contract that pays only on the lost evening, on the same market and with the same fees, raises the worst-of-twenty season by 1 to 3 percent of revenue at all ten venues. The timing mismatch is firmly established; the dollar gains rest on reconstructed revenues. The binding constraint is contract design, not price or buyer sophistication.

detail.abstract:
The use of state-or county-wide comparisons within the United States can either mask differences within a state or lead to an overwhelming number to compare. This work makes use of existing sources of information to identify named regions as a set of counties based on shared cultural, economic, geographic and political characteristics within each state. These regions are adjusted to be largely consistent with federally-defined area designations and sized to be used for meaningful comparison at a national scale. The result is 263 state regions with most states having between four and seven regions. Nine states, primarily in the Northeast, have fewer than four regions and five states, led by Texas with 13, have more than seven. 

In identifying regions within each state we seek to be consistent with federally-defined areas. The result is that 98% of counties (or county equivalents) for Metropolitan and Micropolitan Statistical Areas are within the same state region. 95% of the counties within federallydefined commuting zones are in the same region as the county of the largest city in the zone. We find that roughly 15% of counties belong to overlapping regions. For these counties, we note the overlap but identify a primary region for purposes of analysis and mapping. 

We examine the size of each identified region based upon the number of counties it contains, its population and its area. The largest region in terms of number of counties is the High Plains region of Texas. The Greater Los Angeles region of California has the largest population and the Interior region of Alaska has the largest area. As part of our methodology, we also use the product of population and area of each region to identify and combine roughly 10% of regions that were originally identified. These regions were too small for comparison on a national scale. 

The 263 state regions reduces the number of areas to consider by more than an order of magnitude relative to the number of counties and increases the number by more than a half order of magnitude relative to the number of states. This number represents an intermediate level of granularity that can be helpful for comparison on a national scale relative to the coarse granularity of states and relatively fine granularity of counties. 

We illustrate the use of state regions for two comparisons of data on a national scale. Our first comparison makes use of a classic study on regional variation in the U.S. for the use of "pop" vs. "soda" terms when referring to soft drinks. We reproduce a well-known map with county-level results and compare it to a region-level map of the same data. The result is a clearer delineation of soft drink areas of the the U.S. so that low and no data counties do not show as outliers.

Our second comparison examines an important demographic statistic, U.S. population growth, at the state, county and region levels. In contrast to the “too few” state or “too many” county results, maps based on regions show an intermediate level of detail, which provide the best tradeoff of showing national variation while also capturing regional variation within states.

Interactive versions of all maps generated and shown in this report can be viewed with a Web browser at the project website. The site also contains a downloadable dataset with a list of all counties (or equivalents) and their mapping to a primary region (and secondary if applicable). A separate file of regions can also be downloaded. The project website can be accessed at: https://web.cs.wpi.edu/%7ecew/stateregions/.

detail.abstract:
THE EXECUTIVE QUESTION: How do we give autonomous AI enough freedom to create enterprise value without giving it unbounded authority to create enterprise risk, and how do we let the controls the enterprise already operates work at the speed of the agents?

THE IDEA IN BRIEF

The problem. AI agents are moving from answering questions to taking actions. Second Line’s instruments (policies, limits, exception processes, monitoring, challenge) are typically operated through documents, periodic testing, and human review. Approving every action destroys the value of autonomy; embedding rules in every application fragments control.

The proposal. One reusable boundary between agents and the enterprise, through which Second Line, an existing function, makes corporate standards enforceable. Before a consequential action takes effect, the boundary checks it against versioned policy and the agent’s delegated authority, then allows, modifies, holds, escalates, or blocks it.

The result. Routine work stays autonomous. Human judgment goes where it adds control value. Every decision the boundary makes traces to its policy, or to the default rule where policy is silent.


This paper proposes a reusable runtime control architecture for scaling agentic AI while preserving bounded enterprise authority. The architecture combines a governed semantic layer and Bounded Data Contract with a runtime control plane that evaluates proposed autonomous actions against context, delegated authority, applicable policy, system state, and risk conditions before they become consequential enterprise effects. Rather than embedding every enterprise risk rule within individual applications, the model creates a shared evaluation boundary capable of allowing, modifying, holding, escalating, or blocking proposed actions.

The paper also proposes an institutional operating model in which First-Line technology and business functions retain ownership of execution while selected Second-Line risk boundaries become machine-enforceable at the point of action, with Internal Audit remaining the independent Third Line. Telemetry closes the control loop by making interventions, outcomes, exceptions, and policy performance observable and testable.

Finally, the paper introduces an Agentic AI Readiness Framework and four testable enterprise hypotheses for evaluating whether runtime governance can improve risk containment, operational efficiency, governance cycle time, and adaptive control. The paper's contribution is not a new technical primitive, but an operational synthesis of semantic control, delegated authority, runtime policy enforcement, graduated intervention, institutional risk authority, and evidence into a control architecture for governable autonomy.

detail.abstract:
Do sophisticated investors update their beliefs faster or more slowly when uncertainty rises? Information-cost accounts of partial adjustment, including rational inattention, predict faster updating; a cost of abandoning a model-based benchmark that rises with uncertainty predicts the opposite. In the credit-default-swap market, after the largest widening jumps, spreads do not reverse in calm months but reverse when aggregate uncertainty is high-a three-month difference of about 8 per cent of the spread. Tightening jumps show a much weaker effect. Belief surprises forecast a partial reversal of spreads, and that reversal is weaker in highuncertainty months, as the friction predicts, yet the estimate is imprecise and fades once common monthly shocks are removed. With only 25 changes of the uncertainty state, the data cannot distinguish the absence of this slower correction from its presence; the evidence on it is directional, not decisive.

The replication package for this paper is available at Harvard Dataverse: https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/RV9OCI

detail.abstract: Background: Farmers who handle pesticides often report multiple co-occurring health complaints, yet occupational health research typically analyzes each complaint separately. This study used latent class analysis (LCA) to identify person-centered subgroups of pesticide-exposed farmers based on their patterns of health complaints and their sociodemographic and psychosocial correlates. Methods: This cross-sectional study analyzed 200 farmers with complete data from five villages of Nagari Balimbiang, West Sumatra, Indonesia (June 2026). Six binary health complaints were entered into one- to five-class latent class models estimated by expectation-maximization, with model selection based on information criteria, entropy, and classification-accuracy diagnostics. Bivariate tests and multivariable logistic regression identified correlates of class membership. Results: A two-class solution fit best (BIC = 1215.70; entropy R² = 0.941). Class 1, high multisystem burden (n = 18, 9.0%), showed near-universal musculoskeletal and respiratory complaints and high dermatological, ocular, poisoning, and helminthic probabilities; Class 2, low-to-moderate burden (n = 182, 91.0%), showed markedly lower probabilities across all complaints. The high-burden class had higher attitude (p = 0.0004) and social support (p = 0.022) in bivariate analysis; in multivariable regression, only social support remained independently associated with high-burden membership (adjusted odds ratio 1.18, 95% CI 1.01-1.36, p = 0.031). Conclusions: A small subgroup (approximately 9%) of farmers carries a disproportionate multisystem health burden not explained by lower knowledge, attitude, or safety behavior, but by higher social support, suggesting reverse causation. Symptom-based case-finding embedded in agricultural extension and primary care, leveraging existing family and peer-support networks, may help identify and refer this high-burden minority.

affiliations: Harvard University

detail.title: A Covariance Identity for Marginal Rényi Entropy of Planar Convex Bodies

declarations.funderStatement: Funding for this research was provided in part by Harvard Business School.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Harvard Business School Working Paper No. 27-031

detail.abstract: For a uniform point X in a convex polygon and every 0 < α < ∞, we prove the covariance identity (r_α + r_α″)/r_α = −α Cov(g′, k′) away from directions normal to edges. Here r_α(θ) = exp h_α(⟨u_θ, X⟩), where u_θ = (cos θ, sin θ) and h_α is Rényi entropy; derivatives of r_α are angular, while g′ and k′ are respectively the upper and lower boundary slopes when the projection direction is taken as the horizontal axis. The covariance is taken under the density proportional to the α-th power of the chord length and is nonpositive because the slopes are oppositely monotone. Together with an explicit derivative-jump formula at edge normals, the identity gives a new proof that, for X uniform on any planar convex body, the functional v ↦ exp h_α(⟨v, X⟩), extended by 0 at the origin, is a norm for every 0 ≤ α ≤ ∞. A corresponding one-sided measure inequality for arbitrary planar convex bodies yields a geometric characterization: at each finite positive order, the unit ball under this norm is a polygon if and only if the original body is a triangle, in which case the unit ball is a centrally symmetric hexagon.

detail.title: Comment on "AI in Ophthalmology: A Bibliometric Analysis of Retinal Imaging Innovations and Global Research Collaboration": Methodological Scrutiny, Technological Paradigms, and Translational Imperatives
detail.abstract: This study examines the methodological foundations, research trends, and translational challenges of artificial intelligence (AI)-based retinal imaging applications in clinical ophthalmology. The objective was to critically evaluate how bibliometric research has characterized AI developments in major sight-threatening retinal diseases, including diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, retinal vein occlusion, and glaucomatous optic neuropathy, while identifying limitations that influence the interpretation of current evidence. This commentary analyzed existing bibliometric approaches, focusing on database selection, search strategies, collaboration patterns, and the gap between computational performance and clinical applicability. The assessment highlighted important concerns related to inconsistent dataset coverage, differences between Scopus and Web of Science indexing, the inclusion of non-peer-reviewed studies, unequal international research participation, and limited representation of populations with high disease burden. The findings indicate that although AI models have achieved remarkable diagnostic accuracy, their clinical integration remains restricted by dataset variability, fairness issues, limited interpretability, and regulatory challenges. The review also outlines the evolution of retinal AI technologies from conventional convolutional neural networks to vision transformers, self-supervised foundation models, and multimodal vision-language systems. In conclusion, future retinal AI research should prioritize transparent methodologies, diverse clinical datasets, equitable collaborations, and robust validation pathways to ensure that technological advances translate into reliable, accessible, and patient-centered ophthalmic care.

detail.abstract:
​Background: Accurate perioperative staging guides treatment decision-making in gastric cancer (GC). However, CT-based staging remains suboptimal. This study aimed to develop and validate a deep learning framework for automated gastric tumor segmentation and T/N staging.

Methods: This multicenter real-world study enrolled GC patients undergoing gastrectomy at nine hospitals in China. Gastric Automated Sensing and Recognition Technology for Oncology Neural Engine (GastroSense AI), a combined segmentation and classification framework, was developed and externally validated on volumetric contrast-enhanced CT data using 3D deep learning architectures. Segmentation performance was evaluated by the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), and classification performance for T stage (four categories) and N stage (two categories) by overall accuracy. Model predictions were compared with radiologists' assessments in a prospective cohort.

Findings: A total of 6,742 patients were included, comprising 2,735 in the development cohort and 4,007 in eight external validation cohorts. The segmentation model achieved a mean DSC of 0·76 in the internal test cohort and 0·66-0·79 across external cohorts. The T-stage model achieved accuracies of 62·2% in the internal cohort and 51·0%-63·0% across external cohorts, while the N-stage model achieved accuracies of 75·3% and 54·5%-78·6%, respectively. In the prospective comparative cohort (n=284), the T- and N-stage models demonstrated significantly higher accuracy than radiologists, with relative improvements of 69·7% and 11·0%, respectively (P<0·001 and P=0·026).

Interpretation: GastroSense AI enables automated tumor segmentation as well as standardized and accurate CT-based staging in GC. Visualization software was developed to support preoperative assessment and decision-making.

detail.abstract: We introduce an ex ante valuation budget into CEO compensation design with participation and incentive compatibility. With affine utility and ordered payoff bounds, the least-cost contract is generically bang-bang, and a positive affordability shadow value makes valuation weights shape incentive allocation. U.S. panel evidence links financial tightness to lower option shares and growth opportunities to higher shares, including within option-bearing packages; individually classified awards corroborate these associations. Finally, conventional-call illustrations show that option-bearing pay can fit within budget when purely linear pay cannot; under a binding cap, reoptimizing action and call quantity yields an option share near its empirical mean.

detail.abstract: Why do institutional configurations that successfully support productive transformation at one point in time sometimes become less effective as economies evolve? Existing research has shown that institutions matter for development, that similar economic functions can be performed by different institutional forms, and that the constraints facing growth change over time. Yet these insights remain fragmented across institutional economics, development economics and comparative capitalism. This paper develops a framework of functional institutional mismatch to analyse the alignment between the functional capacities supplied or made accessible by an institutional configuration and the evolving requirements of productive transformation. The framework distinguishes five interdependent capacities: appropriation, coordination, experimentation, reallocation and adaptation. It is applied through a structured comparative analysis of Malaysia, Morocco, Türkiye and the United Arab Emirates, four Muslim-majority economies with markedly different institutional configurations and productive trajectories. The comparison suggests that strong coordination capacity can support investment, industrialisation and diversification but is insufficient for sustained productivity upgrading when experimentation, firm scaling and resource reallocation remain constrained. It also shows that required capacities need not be generated domestically: the UAE illustrates how external sourcing of capital, technology, entrepreneurship and skills can contribute to continued functional alignment when combined with strong coordination and adaptation. The paper argues that development constraints may emerge not because institutions become uniformly weaker, but because their functional profiles cease to match the changing requirements of productive transformation.

detail.abstract:
Background: Assisted reproductive technology (ART) is increasingly used worldwide, yet the long-term reproductive consequences of repeated ovarian stimulation (OS), an essential component of ART, remain incompletely understood.

Methods: We conducted a longitudinal cohort study of women with normal ovarian reserve who underwent ART between 2008 and 2017. Cumulative OS exposure was assessed by the number of OS cycles and cumulative gonadotropin dose. Serum anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) and antral follicle count (AFC) were measured before OS and repeatedly during follow-up, and diminished ovarian reserve (DOR) was defined as AMH <1·1 ng/mL. Linear mixed-effects models were used to evaluate the association between cumulative OS exposure and longitudinal ovarian reserve, and multivariable logistic regression was used to examine the association between cumulative OS exposure and incident DOR, adjusting for age, follow-up time, BMI, baseline AMH, infertility duration, and infertility type.

Findings: Among 9,470 participants, 8,034 underwent one OS cycle, 1,184 underwent two cycles, and 252 underwent three or more cycles. In adjusted models, women who underwent two OS cycles (β = −0·05; 95% CI, −0·09 to −0·02) or three or more OS cycles (β = −0·28; 95% CI, −0·35 to −0·22) had lower longitudinal AMH levels and more rapid relative declines than those who underwent one OS cycle. They also had higher odds of incident DOR (OR, 1·47; 95% CI, 1·19 to 1·81 for two cycles; OR, 2·47; 95% CI, 1·71 to 3·56 for three or more cycles). AFC showed generally consistent trends. Among women who underwent one OS cycle, those in the highest quartile of cumulative gonadotropin dose (Q4, 2150–7050 IU) had higher odds of incident DOR than those in the lowest quartile (Q1, 0–1237·5 IU) (OR, 1·50; 95% CI, 1·14 to 1·97). The highest OR for incident DOR was observed among women receiving >1500 IU for <10 days, compared with those receiving ≤1500 IU for ≥10 days (OR, 2·21; 95% CI, 1·47 to 3·33).

Interpretation: A greater number of OS cycles and higher gonadotropin doses were associated with lower longitudinal AMH levels, more rapid relative declines in AMH, and an increased risk of DOR among women with normal ovarian reserve, suggesting a potential dose-response relationship between cumulative OS exposure and ovarian ageing. These findings identify OS as a potential correlate of reproductive ageing and highlight the importance of incorporating cumulative OS exposure into individualized reproductive counseling and health management for women undergoing ART.

detail.abstract:
Background: Streptococcus pneumoniae remains a major cause of morbidity, mortality, and healthcare expenditure among U.S. adults despite the availability of effective vaccines. Although pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) have reduced disease incidence, the overall health and economic burden of pneumococcal disease in adults under evolving vaccination policies remains incompletely characterized.

Methods: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 and CHEERS 2022 guidelines and registered in PROSPERO(CRD420251145014). Six databases (PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Embase) were searched for U.S. studies published between 2010 and February 2025. Eligible studies included economic evaluations, cost-of-illness analyses, or budget impact studies of pneumococcal disease or vaccination among adults ≥18 years. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment. Due to methodological heterogeneity across studies, economic outcomes were synthesized narratively.

Results: Forty studies met inclusion criteria. Most studies (n=28) used Markov or probabilistic cohort models, 29 adopted lifetime time horizons, and 37 applied a 3% annual discount rate. PCV13 generally demonstrated dominance or favorable incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) compared with PPSV23. PCV15 showed modest improvements in cost-effectiveness compared with PCV20 or the sequential PCV15+PPSV23 strategy, depending on pricing assumptions. PCV20 consistently emerged as the most economically favorable single-dose strategy, while PCV21 further extended cost-effectiveness in both age- and race-stratified populations compared with PCV15+PPSV23. Only one study suggested PCV24 may be economically less favorable than PCV21. Overall methodological quality was moderate to high.

Discussion: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccination represents a high-value, cost-effective intervention for U.S. adults, particularly with higher-valency vaccines such as PCV20 and PCV21.

detail.abstract:
Coercive, non-pro rata debt restructurings, often driven by private equity sponsors, have become a major force for fixing distressed companies. They are promoted—by stressed companies, their owners, their advisors, and favored creditors—as the best way to avoid bankruptcy and reduce financial stress by extending distressed firms’ runways to recover and take off. If true, it would explain their growing frequency. But the post-deal results contradict proponents’ positive claims.

First, a majority of coercively restructured firms end up filing for bankruptcy anyway—a letdown for a maneuver mainly justified as avoiding bankruptcy. Second, the winning participants typically take higher-priority debt rather than stabilizing equity, thereby further undermining already overindebted structures. High debt levels and low credit ratings persist. The added capital complexity prods the firm toward default and a potentially a thornier bankruptcy. Third, efficiency justifications commonly offered—like avoiding bankruptcy’s expense—are doubtful. Coercive debt restructurings are themselves expensive, and many restructured firms end up in bankruptcy anyway, yielding two costly deals. Fourth, coercive restructurings are as consistent with redistributing value from disfavored creditors to owners and favored creditors as with efficient restructuring.

We present evidence supporting all four claims. As such, coercive recapitalizations may lock capital in less-than-worthwhile investments for longer than is efficient. From a lawyer’s perspective, that could raise troubling fiduciary-duty questions. From a market-wide perspective, inefficient recapitalizations and capital misallocation could eventually favor more effective contractual terms and deals. Rent-seeking to grab value from other investors can persist despite its costs, but not always.

detail.abstract: The U.S.-China trade war in 2018-19 was bilateral in nature, but its effects extended to countries linked to both economies through global supply chains. This paper studies how the trade war affected Korea, a bystander country deeply integrated with China and the United States. While existing evidence on bystander countries emphasizes rerouting and trade diversion, Korea imported less from China after the trade war. We develop a simple analytical model of a global supply chain linking China, Korea, and the United States. The model shows that U.S. tariffs can reduce Korean imports from China when Chinese production exhibits increasing returns to scale: lower Chinese sales to the U.S. contract production scale, raise Chinese marginal costs, and increase the prices Korean firms pay for Chinese goods. The model also allows Chinese producers to reroute goods through Korea, generating heterogeneous effects across sectors depending on rerouting costs. Using transaction-level Korean customs data, we find that a 10 percentage-point increase in U.S. tariffs on Chinese products reduced Korean import quantities from China by about 24 percent and raised Korean import prices by about 2.5 percent. The decline is concentrated in industries exhibiting increasing returns to scale. However, in industries with high pre-shock U.S.-export exposure, Korean imports from China and exports to the U.S. both rise, consistent with rerouting through Korea. These results show that bilateral tariffs can generate both decoupling from China and indirect China-U.S. trade through third countries.

detail.abstract:
Data centers provide essential information processing, access, storage, and interconnection for the Internet and other broadband networks. In a short period of time, these networks have changed substantially in terms of their physical location, size, ownership, primary functions, capacity, resource requirements, and public perception. This paper tracks the history of data centers, with emphasis on whether developers can successfully migrate from large terrestrial footprints to space orbits. 

 The paper explains how and why the Court of Public Opinion has shifted from indifference to extraordinary, bipartisan opposition,  despite the need for ever more capacity to handle growing demands from Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) applications.  It also assesses whether orbiting data center (“ODC”) development can avoid triggering similar opposition, despite the potential for generating less environmental harm and infrastructure burdens.

The paper explains that having less adverse impacts on specific localities, ODCs can likely exacerbate chronic and emerging problems that can thwart or impede robust global commercial space commerce.  The paper recommends ODC developers enhance their reputation in international, intergovernmental, and national space governance forums by prioritizing research and advocacy on ways to solve a growing list of space sustainability challenges.

detail.abstract:
East Africa’s next digital transformation challenge is not building more infrastructure. It is connecting fragmented public and private systems, making them intelligent enough to understand economic behavior, and programmable enough to execute trusted transactions across borders. This paper argues that cross-border trade friction in the East African Community (EAC) is a multi-layer interoperability failure, and that the arrival of programmable money (central bank digital currencies, global and local stablecoins, and tokenized deposits) introduces a paradox: each instrument can resolve a liquidity or settlement gap while fragmenting the monetary layer itself.
We make four contributions. First, we formalize the Programmable Money Paradox, showing that adding settlement instruments without a shared interoperability fabric increases the number of conversion edges a trader must traverse. Second, we propose a six-layer interoperability framework spanning payment, identity, data, regulatory, AI and money interoperability. Third, we develop the concept of Behavioral Economic Intelligence (BEI), the privacy-preserving transformation of firm-level transaction signals into trade-relevant inferences on creditworthiness, liquidity, compliance risk and supply-chain timing. Fourth, we specify the East African Intelligent Interoperability Index (EA-I3), a composite measure across seven pillars that enables comparison of partner states and tracks progress of initiatives such as the Rwanda–Tanzania linkage of TIPS and RSwitch.
We close with testable propositions, a governance agenda for federated AI across jurisdictions, and a research program for empirical validation.

detail.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents (systems that couple a language model with tools, memory, and orchestration so that they can plan and act with limited supervision) are entering production just as the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) and Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) begin to apply. Both instruments impose binding cybersecurity duties, yet both articulate outcome-oriented obligations rather than implementable safeguards, leaving providers, auditors, and market-surveillance authorities without a shared technical baseline. This article bridges that gap. Using doctrinal analysis, we decompose the cybersecurity-relevant provisions of the AI Act (Articles 9-15, 53, 55, and 72-73) and the CRA (Articles 13-14 and Annex I) into discrete obligation atoms, and we map each atom to concrete technical controls for LLM-based autonomous agents drawn from established control catalogues and recent agent-security research. The mapping is organised around an agentspecific threat model (prompt injection, tool poisoning, memory and retrieval poisoning, excessive agency, privacy attacks, and supply-chain compromise) and specifies, for every control, the verification evidence that supports conformity assessment and enforcement. We show how the CRA's deemed-compliance mechanism can operationalise the AI Act's cybersecurity requirement, analyse the enforcement timeline as amended in 2026, and identify residual gaps where neither instrument nor pending harmonised standards adequately captures agentic behaviour. The resulting obligation-to-control matrix offers a testable baseline for demonstrating, and enforcing, compliance.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence presents an unusually difficult problem for global governance. The technology develops rapidly, crosses borders easily, and is shaped by actors whose resources and capabilities may rival those of states. Yet international responses remain fragmented, unevenly representative, and overwhelmingly non-binding. The challenge is therefore not simply to identify appropriate rules or institutions, but to understand who has the capacity and incentive to create, enforce, and adapt them.

This review essay examines these questions through Matthijs Maas’s Architectures of Global AI Governance. Maas offers an ambitious framework for thinking about AI governance through the lenses of sociotechnical change, governance disruption, and regime complexity. His account usefully resists both technological determinism and the search for a single institutional blueprint, emphasizing instead the possibilities of a fragmented and evolving governance architecture.

The essay argues, however, that institutional design cannot be separated from the distribution of power. Maas frequently invokes what “we” should do about AI, but that collective subject obscures important differences among states, international institutions, and technology companies. States retain formidable powers over markets, infrastructure, strategic inputs, and firms themselves. At the same time, many consequential decisions about frontier AI — what is built, how quickly, with what safeguards, and when it is released — are concentrated within a small number of private companies. The central problem of global AI governance may therefore be less architecture without an architect than an emerging architecture shaped by multiple actors possessing different forms of power, divergent incentives, and no common set of plans.

detail.abstract:
Despite widespread references to information processing as occurring in a cloud, terrestrial data centers provide essential infrastructure.  The largest of these facilities require massive amounts of electric power, coolant, and real estate measured in gigawatts, millions of gallons, and square miles respectively. The expectation that Artificial Intelligence will become essential and transformative throughout the economy and society, has generated insatiable demand for what data centers offer, accommodated by ever larger “hyperscale” installations.

The Court of Public Opinion has pivoted from indifference to substantial opposition. Not in my backyard concerns about nearby environmental harm is shifting to more strident “not on my planet you bastards” as residential and small business consumers of electricity, water, and housing attribute blame data centers for higher costs.

 Launching data centers into space appears to solve, or at least mitigate, several costly terrestrial problems.  In sun synchronous, low Earth orbit, data centers may have comparatively less environmental impact and lower operating costs in two increasingly expensive categories: the gigawatts of electricity continuously required to power components, and coolants, such as water and glycol, needed to syphon away heat generated by constant operation. However, these comparative advantages may disappear entirely, or decline significantly, when other higher expenses and the risks of multi-faceted government regulation enter the total cost calculation.

 This article examines whether orbiting data centers (“ODCs”) can become commercially viable within a few years, a decade, or never.  It also considers whether and how ODCs will bolster prospects for a robust and lucrative new space commerce market development, despite significant chronic, emerging, and theoretical impediments that have been ignored, considered unlikely to ever occur, or underestimated in severity.

detail.abstract: We investigate the effectiveness of artificial intelligences (AI)—specifically large language models (LLMs)—relative to human scientists at high-level cognitive tasks in social science such as theory formulation, predictions of novel empirical results, and theory revision in response to new evidence. The research domain was academic discourse regarding gender and race inequality. Our findings, comparing 25 LLMs with 13 senior researchers and 60 doctoral scholars, reveal that the AIs outperformed most humans individually on most of the present tasks, while human theories were more diverse and exhibited greater gains in predictive accuracy from aggregation. AI-generated theories were more extensively elaborated, involving additional theoretical paths and latent variables, and were rated as higher quality than human theories by independent raters blinded to source. However, this theoretical complexity was in part ornamental, in that it was not associated with more accurate predictions about empirical patterns in data; in contrast, human scientists achieved greater predictive efficiency with simpler theories. The AIs were significantly more likely than human scientists to revise their theories to incorporate new evidence; human scientists updated their beliefs in a selective way that is sensitive to prior prediction errors. We speculate that the superior processing capacity of artificial intelligences makes them especially well-suited to tasks requiring grappling with complexity, but that the greater diversity of human ideas is essential to wise crowds and collective creativity.

detail.abstract: Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Apache Hudi are the three dominant open table formats for the data lakehouse, and published performance comparisons among them are unusually inconsistent-a fact the Apache Hudi project's own engineering blog documents in detail, cataloging methodology errors including compression mismatches, misapplied write operations, undersized datasets, and stale version references in prior published benchmarks. This paper synthesizes the current, most transparent public record, drawing primarily on a reproducible August 2026 benchmark from the Apache Hudi project using an open-source, format-agnostic harness (LakeLoader) across current versions (Hudi 1.1.1, Iceberg 1.10.0, Delta Lake 3.3.2). On a 10 TB skewed mutation-heavy facttable workload, that benchmark reports Hudi's incremental write latency roughly 4x lower than Iceberg and 6x lower than Delta Lake; on a wide, sparsely-updated dimension-table workload, roughly 8x lower than Iceberg and 5x lower than Delta Lake. By contrast, a corrected 2022 TPC-DS scan-heavy benchmark, rerun after identifying configuration-parity errors in an earlier comparison, found load performance within 6% between Hudi and Delta Lake with no material difference in query performance-indicating that table format choice matters most for mutation-heavy workloads and least for read-dominated, append-only ones. We present each format's metadata and update-resolution architecture, synthesize the benchmark evidence with explicit attention to its source's stated methodology and acknowledged affiliation with one of the projects compared, and propose a workload-based decision framework together with an evaluation methodology for teams selecting a table format for their own environment.

detail.abstract: Published asset-pricing factors are measurements of a latent factor structure, and measurements have error. Using a spectral estimator that reads a factor's measurement-error variance off the top eigenstructure of a return panel, we grade thirteen published factors (the Fama-French five, momentum, AQR's quality, betting-against-beta and monthly-updated value, and the four q-factors) against four static test-asset universes and against conditional universes estimated by instrumented PCA and a conditional autoencoder. Each characteristic factor measures its own sort well and everything else poorly: momentum is a 97%-pure, nearly noise-free measurement on its own 25 size/momentum portfolios and barely visible elsewhere, only the market is clean everywhere, and a placebo rules out a sorting tautology. On individual stocks, conditioning raises momentum's spanning R2 from 0.33 to 0.70-0.77, a gain that holds out of sample in both time directions, while value moves the other way. Feeding the measured noise into errors-in-variables-corrected two-pass regressions cuts the profitability premium from 5.3 to 1.7 percent per year, with a joint-bootstrap band of [1.4, 2.0]; the whole zoo can be corrected jointly only up to 16 percent of its measured noise, where the implied true-factor covariance turns singular. A point-in-time rebuild of the stock universe shows that the survivor design flattered the characteristic factors by up to 0.11 of spanning R2. A noise-injection experiment on the real panels calibrates the error bars without the simulation prior, with 90% multipliers of 2.4 to 10.5 bootstrap standard errors by universe, and no classification changes. Macro factor candidates fail the spanning screen in static and conditional spaces. Because mean-zero construction noise leaves a factor's mean unchanged and divides its t-statistic by the square root of one plus the noise variance, a factor can replicate and still be a poor measurement.

detail.abstract: Forecasts of the difference between day-ahead and real-time electricity prices (the DART spread) can inform trading and risk assessment. Short price histories make it difficult to estimate reliable forecasting relationships. We test whether histories from other markets can help. We compare five forecasting methods spanning regularized linear models, tree ensembles, and a lag-based sequence model, using data from 13 Chinese provincial markets and restricting the target-market estimation window to 30 or 90 delivery days. External histories significantly reduce mean absolute error (MAE) for three of the five methods. For these methods, cross-market forecasts formed with a 30-day target-market estimation window outperform local-only forecasts formed with a 90-day window by 7–11% in MAE. Of the other two methods, one shows small, statistically insignificant gains. The other improves in most market–month comparisons, but large losses in a minority of comparisons increase its average MAE. We then compare two ways to use local data alongside external histories. Joint training brings no consistent further accuracy gain. Alternatively, combining a separate Local forecast with the cross-market forecast can improve performance consistency across markets and months. In the main combination comparison, it reduces both the frequency and magnitude of shortfalls relative to Local. Overall, external histories can improve point-forecast accuracy with short local estimation windows, while forecast combination can help limit occasional losses from cross-market forecasting. These gains do not establish better prediction of extreme spreads.

detail.abstract: This article examines the scope of the provision that excludes transactions, mediation, and special tax and customs arbitration from the revenue waiver regime provided for in Article 14 of the Fiscal Responsibility Law. Through a legal-dogmatic and documentary analysis, it interprets Article 171-C of the National Tax Code in continuity with prior legislation and distinguishes between tax classification, authorization to dispose of the tax credit, and the measurement of its effects. It argues that the unity of tax treatment does not eliminate the differences between a negotiated settlement, an assisted consensual resolution, and an adjudication. It develops a criterion of functional autonomy to examine the benefits inherent in settlement programs, while preserving the concessions that form part of the agreement. Based on this distinction, it addresses constitutional controls and the relationship with Article 14-A of tax legislation. It demonstrates that face value, net book value, ability to pay, and expected recovery address distinct questions. Functional comparison and the experience of external oversight underpin the parameters of justification and disclosure. It concludes that the specific classification must produce its own effect, while the remaining controls apply according to their respective premises.

detail.abstract: As the companion paper to our CBAM analysis, this study examines the supply chain compliance costs and macroeconomic consequences of EU Reg ulation (EU) 2023/1542—the EU Battery Regulation—for the Guangdong Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA), which supplies approximately 38% of EU EV battery demand. Three regulatory scenarios— Light (BR-L), Moderate (BR-M), and Strict (BR-S)—are simulated over 2025–2034. Under BR-S, total compliance costs reach approximately 36% of baseline production cost by 2034 (direct costs 18%, management 10.5%, supply chain reconfiguration 7.5%). Battery sector carbon emissions decline 12 38% relative to baseline. CBAM–Battery Regulation interaction generates positive complementarities: carbon reduction synergies reduce CBAM liabil ity, and shared LCA infrastructure saves 30–45% of management compliance costs. Five targeted policy implications are derived.

detail.abstract: Big data is increasingly central to corporate economic decision-making. However, whether energy-related data platforms expand firms’ sustainability-related knowledge boundaries remains unclear. Using data from Chinese A-share listed manufacturing firms from 2015 to 2024, we exploit the establishment of provincial-level energy big data centers as a quasi-natural experiment and show that these centers promote exploratory green innovation. The main results remain robust to a battery of checks. We further identify government environmental subsidies as a key mechanism, and find that the effect is stronger for firms with higher-quality environmental governance and disclosure. Heterogeneity analyses reveal stronger innovation effects among firms with higher levels of digital transformation, a stronger managerial long-term orientation, less favorable green reputations, more stringent environmental regulation, or greater exposure to extreme heat. These findings provide empirical evidence on how field-specific big data expands corporate technological boundaries and offer implications for governments and firms seeking to improve resource-allocation efficiency through big data platforms.

detail.abstract: Do supply-driven oil-price increases affect the international supply of dollar credit to oil-importing economies? We combine two published measures of oil supply disturbances with BIS locational banking positions vis-à-vis China. Instrumenting oil returns withBaumeister–Hamilton supply shocks, we find that a 1 percent supply-induced increase in oil prices raises international banks’ dollar claims on Chinese banks by 0.34 percent within the quarter. Känzig’s independently identified oil-supply-news shocks produce a comparable response of 0.23 percent. The adjustment is concentrated in claims on banks: dollar liabilities do not expand, and claims on nonbanks respond less. The increase subsequently reverses, consistent with temporary funding accommodation rather than permanent credit creation. Complementary evidence links larger oil-import bills to more negative CNY–dollar cross-currency bases, although the short modern sample limits causal inference for this price response. The findings identify a bank-intermediation channel through which commodity supply disturbances propagate into the international dollar system.

title: When Carbon Footprints Mislead Policy: Climate-Policy Ranking Reversals and the Missing Handprint

detail.title: When Carbon Footprints Mislead Policy: Climate-Policy Ranking Reversals and the Missing Handprint
detail.abstract: This study examines when a correctly measured carbon footprint can become an incomplete signal for ranking climate policy. We develop a two-country stochastic real-options model in which footprint-based policy changes the relative price and adoption of a climate-positive technology, while downstream avoided emissions—the technology’s carbon handprint—remain outside private valuation. This boundary mismatch generates distinct private and climate-adjusted investment thresholds and a missing-handprint region in which socially warranted investment is privately delayed. A policy-ranking reversal occurs when the downstream handprint exceeds the production-footprint disadvantage and the policy-induced reduction in adoption worsens the full climate outcome. We calibrate the model to Chinese battery electric vehicles entering the European Union market and solve the investment problem using Monte Carlo and least-squares Monte Carlo methods. A stochastic reversal-frontier analysis identifies the states in which footprint and full-climate rankings diverge, while global sensitivity analysis shows that reversal risk is driven by interactions among downstream abatement, adoption responsiveness, market uncertainty, and policy uncertainty rather than by any single parameter. The results do not imply that footprint regulation should be abandoned. Instead, they show that policy stringency should be calibrated with attention to deployment responses when material climate benefits occur beyond the production-accounting boundary.

detail.abstract: Abstract: This study examines the impact of urban digitalisation on corporate carbon emissions by exploiting the staggered rollout of China’s National Smart City Pilot Program as a quasi-natural experiment. Using a staggered difference-in-differences (DID) framework based on panel data of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2010 to 2024, we find that urban digitalisation significantly reduces corporate carbon emissions by approximately 4.86%. This finding remains robust after a comprehensive battery of robustness checks, including dynamic parallel trend tests, placebo tests, alternative measures of carbon intensity, alternative staggered DID estimators based on CSDID and stacked DID approaches, Goodman–Bacon decomposition, double machine learning, instrumental variable estimation, and PSM-DID. Mechanism analyses reveal that urban digitalisation facilitates corporate decarbonization through two transmission pathways: reducing information frictions by lowering demand uncertainty and improving supply chain operational efficiency, and strengthening government environmental governance by enhancing green policy attention and environmental regulatory enforcement. Furthermore, heterogeneity analyses show that the emission reduction effect is more pronounced in cities with stronger digital infrastructure, among firms in highly polluting industries, and among firms facing lower financial constraints. Overall, this study provides micro-level evidence on how digital public infrastructure promotes corporate decarbonization and highlights the critical roles of information efficiency and environmental governance in facilitating low-carbon transitions. Keywords: Digital public infrastructure; Corporate carbon emissions; Smart city policy; Information frictions; Green transitionJEL Classification: Q54; Q55; Q58; O33

detail.abstract: This paper empirically investigates the macroeconomic and institutional determinants of national fiscal rule adoption using a comprehensive panel dataset of 130 developed and emerging countries from 1990 to 2020. Moving beyond aggregate metrics, we model fiscal rule implementation as a discrete binary choice using a random-effects Probit estimator to account for heterogeneity across budget balance, debt, expenditure, and revenue rules. Our findings reveal that a core set of variables-including inflation-targeting monetary regimes, hard-fixed exchange rates, the presence of sovereign wealth funds, and higher overall economic development-systematically increases the probability of rule adoption, whereas demographic pressures deter it. Crucially, the preconditions for adoption vary significantly by rule type; for instance, strong democratic institutions facilitate the adoption of debt and budget balance rules, whereas substantial oil rents hinder the adoption of debt and revenue rules but support budget balance constraints. Finally, applying our predictive models to contemporary data identifies significant global policy gaps, highlighting several advanced and resource-rich economies that possess the structural fundamentals for fiscal rules yet currently operate without them.

detail.abstract: Assessments of critical-raw-material capacity commonly combine physical production and trade statistics as if they provided mutually consistent measures of the same underlying phenomenon. Wartime conditions make this assumption particularly problematic. This paper examines how robust measured assessments of Ukraine's critical-raw-material economy are once units, official data vintages, territorial discontinuities and trade-reporting conventions are explicitly reconciled. The analysis focuses on natural graphite, ilmenite and leucoxene, and marketable manganese ore. It combines a reconstructed physical-production index for 2010-2024, a calibrated resource-contribution accounting decomposition of real GDP, and constant-market-share analysis of corresponding mineral trade. The reconstruction materially alters several previously reported results. For 2014-2021, the estimated CRM accounting contribution remains positive but modest, at approximately 0.13 percentage points per year; alternative fixed price weights raise it to 0.25-0.38 percentage points. For 2021-2023, the contribution is strongly negative, at approximately-6.0 percentage points annually, while the non-CRM residual is also negative. In world trade, the residual market-share component is strongly negative for 2018-2023 and remains almost unchanged when the benchmark is restricted to common reporters. In the fixedcomposition EU27 analysis, the residual component is positive for 2018-2023, turns negative through 2024 and is approximately neutral through 2025. Production and trade measures also diverge sharply, including exports despite zero reported contemporaneous mine output and substantial reporter-mirror discrepancies. The results show that data construction is not a secondary technical issue: it can determine the substantive economic narrative assigned to a mineral sector.

detail.abstract: Public administration research often employs aggregate measures such as satisfaction, trust, burnout, and policy acceptability. These scores are often treated as direct proxies for respondents' underlying evaluation criteria: researchers infer the mechanisms behind observed ratings without directly eliciting the judgmental grounds on which respondents form their assessments. One understudied conceptual puzzle emerges from a simple observation: an aggregate evaluation and the criteria used to produce it are distinct constructs, yet measurement practice routinely conflates them. When identical aggregate scores can mask divergent evaluative rationales, we face a foundational question: under what conditions should measurement remain at the aggregate level, rather than probing further into respondents' reasons? This article articulates a measurement challenge underexplored in public administration scholarship. While researchers have developed sophisticated tools for post-hoc scale validation, little practical guidance exists for deciding whether to directly elicit evaluative criteria behind scores-and, if elicitation proceeds, when to stop probing. We introduce the concept of outward extendability of evaluation criteria: when researchers ask respondents to unpack their ratings, respondents can generate increasingly granular justifications iteratively, with no inherent natural stopping point in this chain of reasons. Continued probing can keep revealing finer considerations indefinitely. The argument unfolds in three parts. First, much public administration research reconstructs evaluative criteria from aggregate scores rather than eliciting respondents' own rationales. This habit rests on an unexamined assumption: aggregate ratings and the criteria producing them are interchangeable. This practice persists due to three overlapping influences: revealed-preference reasoning, concerns over selfreport biases, and the practical convenience of standardized surveys. As a corrective, this article proposes a layered elicitation framework paired with a stopping rule anchored in marginal informational gain, contextual stability, and actionable institutional capacity. The framework does not replace aggregate measurement. Instead, it provides a normative basis for deciding when aggregate indicators should be supplemented by direct elicitation of evaluative criteria. The core question is not whether researchers possess the technical ability to keep probing respondents. It is whether the decision to terminate probing at a given layer can be theoretically and empirically justified.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines why the conversion of Crew Transfer Vessels (CTVs) and Offshore Supply Vessels (OSVs) to hybrid-electric propulsion remains uneven despite a demonstrated technical and economic case for the transition. Using a mixed-methods empirical design, the study compares the European Union, where hybrid conversions are increasingly standard on North Sea offshore-wind routes, with the Middle East, where adoption remains marginal despite comparable or superior fuel-price exposure and growing renewable-energy ambition.

Primary data were collected from 120 maritime stakeholders - vessel operators, naval architects, charter principals, classification society surveyors, finance providers, port authorities, and regulators - distributed across the two regions (45 EU, 38 Middle East, 37 dual-region). The instruments combined a structured Likert-scale survey, semi-structured interviews, and documentary review of charter contracts and regulatory filings. Analytical techniques included chi-square tests of independence, independent-samples t-tests, Pearson correlation, and inductive thematic coding of qualitative responses.

The findings establish that the barrier to hybrid conversion in both regions is predominantly structural rather than technical. Converted vessels demonstrate verified fuel savings of 15 to 60 per cent and annual fuel reductions of 500 to 800 tonnes per vessel. However, 70 per cent of respondents cite capital cost as the dominant barrier, with conversion packages ranging from USD 0.5 million to over USD 3 million per vessel and payback periods frequently exceeding charter-contract tenure. The study identifies the misalignment of charter incentives - where the shipowner bears the capital expenditure while the charterer captures the fuel savings - as the single most important structural obstacle, with a chi-square value of 68.47 (p < 0.001) between regulatory posture and conversion outcome. In EU jurisdictions where regulatory support is strong, hybrid-adoption intent reaches 97 per cent; in regulatory environments the study classifies as restrictive or absent, intent falls to zero.

The paper contributes three novel elements to the maritime-decarbonisation literature. First, it is the first large-sample comparative study to isolate the Middle Eastern operating environment as a distinct unit of analysis rather than treating it as part of a wider "rest of the world" aggregate. Second, it provides a quantified decomposition of conversion barriers into technical, financial, regulatory, and contractual components, allowing policy instruments to be targeted at the dominant obstacle rather than at surface symptoms. Third, it proposes a policy framework - the "Charter-Aligned Hybrid Conversion Mechanism" - that reallocates the capital-expenditure/operating-expenditure split through a tripartite instrument involving the owner, the charterer, and either a port authority or an export-credit agency.

detail.abstract: Warren Buffett advised investors to be "fearful when others are greedy" and greedy "only when others are fearful". CNN's Fear & Greed Index is a popular way to see what others feel. It turns seven market measures, such as the S&P 500's momentum, the VIX volatility index and the demand for safe government bonds, into one score from 0 (extreme fear) to 100 (extreme greed). CNN publishes the index only from 2011 and describes its calculation only in words. We rebuilt it from that description back to 2007; our version moves closely with CNN's published values (correlation 0.86). We then turned the advice into a simple rule and tested it on SPY, a fund that holds the S&P 500: buy when the index falls below 25 (Extreme Fear) and sell when it rises above 75 (Extreme Greed). We ran 26 tests from January 2009 to July 2026, each made of 35 six-month periods that were locked on our platform before their results existed. The rule grew 9.3% a year while it held cash half of the time. That was better than the opposite rule, which follows the crowd, and better than the 200-day moving average. Simply holding SPY grew 12.3% a year, and none of the 51 different rules we tested made more than holding its own fund. The buying half of the advice worked: after a day of Extreme Fear, SPY rose more over the next month and the next quarter than after any other level of the index. The selling half did not: after a day of Extreme Greed, SPY rose more over the next year than after any other level, so the rule sold too early and sat in cash while the market kept rising. The rule that did best is the one Buffett recommends for index investors: buy a low-cost S&P 500 fund and keep it.

detail.abstract:
Professional handoffs can preserve the substantive end state of a decision while obscuring how that state differs from the source material from which it was derived. This paper develops a pre-field measurement protocol for one narrow interface problem in complex financial planning: how task-required source-to-handoff transformations are marked in written investment-policy handoffs.

The protocol does not propose a new validated construct. Its primary unit is a Required Transformation Instance (RTI): a frozen source element for which the downstream task requires a transformation rather than verbatim preservation. Receiver outputs are first coded for substantive transformation status and only then for whether a correct transformation is silent, referentially marked, or explicitly marked. A pre-data redundancy gate asks whether every value of the proposed code can be reconstructed from three comparator codings: target-referenced accuracy, source-anchor traceability, and a FRAME-derived modification-documentation codebook. If it can, the standalone line terminates before participant recruitment. Passing this gate is a minimal entry condition, not evidence that the distinction matters.

If the coding distinction survives, Stage 0 has two empirical components. A reproducibility study tests whether the classification can be coded with pre-specified reliability rules. A randomized reader experiment then holds transformed substantive content constant while varying mark form and measures Change-Contingent Action Error (CCAE) in a non-cued downstream task. The design uses explicit FIRE, NOT FIRE, LIMITED, and INCONCLUSIVE states so that null, adverse, redundant, or underpowered results cannot default to survival of the proposed distinction.

Planning simulations are reported only to assess design feasibility. Under the focused five-category reliability scenario used for planning, 150 independent receivers completing two cases each was the first tested configuration in the focused grid to satisfy both the protocol's high-reliability and low-reliability planning targets. Reader-experiment burden was highly sensitive to the smallest effect considered meaningful. These are simulation results under stylized assumptions, not observations about professional practice.

No participants have been recruited. No client or family data are used. The protocol is not preregistered, has not undergone human peer review, and does not claim empirical effectiveness. Its purpose is to define a research object that can be merged, narrowed, or abandoned if established comparators explain the same phenomenon more parsimoniously.

OpenAI ChatGPT and Anthropic Claude were used for literature-discovery support, protocol and manuscript drafting, methods critique, adversarial review, simulation planning, simulation-code drafting assistance, and editorial revision. The author reviewed and edited the resulting material and remains responsible for all research decisions, source verification, code, claims, citations, and final text. AI review was not treated as human peer review, external expert validation, ethics approval, or independent professional endorsement.

detail.abstract: The production function approach estimates markups from output elasticities of flexible inputs and their cost shares in revenue. Recent studies document that markups recovered from different flexible inputs frequently disagree. We show that such conflicting markups arise because standard estimation procedures do not fully exploit the implications of their most prominent maintained assumption-cost minimization. We develop a novel econometric framework that embeds cost-minimization conditions directly into estimation, through cost shares of flexible inputs, while retaining the common Hicks-neutral productivity process. The resulting semi-nonparametric model provides the minimal structure to identify a flexible parameterization of the scale elasticity. Output elasticities can then be recovered from the common scale elasticity via cost minimization, and the resulting markups are invariant across flexible inputs by construction. We show that the key to obtaining invariance in markup estimates is an estimation procedure that enforces consistency of the production function parameters with the optimality conditions of the maintained cost minimization assumption-whether done directly, as in our framework, or indirectly via factor-augmenting productivity. These conclusions are illustrated empirically using manufacturing data from Colombia, Chile, and the United States.

detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Kawasaki disease (KD) is an acquired pediatric cardiovascular disease that can lead to coronary artery aneurysms. Thrombus formation within these aneurysms may cause severe complications, such as myocardial infarction, making early prediction and diagnosis clinically critical. Traditionally, assessment has relied on morphological factors; however, recent studies have reported stronger correlations between thrombus formation and hemodynamic parameters, including time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS). Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) enables quantitative evaluation of these parameters and supports clinical decision-making. However, patient-specific simulations generally require over 12hours and expert involvement, limiting clinical application. This study proposes a machine learning-based super-resolution (SR) reconstruction approach to address this limitation.Methods: The proposed SR approach reconstructs velocity fields from low-resolution (LR) CFD simulations, which require less computation time compared to high-resolution (HR) CFD simulations. The reconstruction performance of the velocity fields and TAWSS was evaluated using leave-one-out cross-validation across patient-specific coronary artery models obtained from 10 KD patients.Results: The integration of machine learning (ML) and CFD reduced the computational time from over 12 hours required for HR CFD to less than 2 hours for LR CFD combined with near-instantaneous SR reconstruction. The ML model mitigated the underestimation of TAWSS in LR CFD simulations, demonstrating robust error reduction across all analyzed vessels without relying on target patient data during training.Conclusions: The proposed super-resolution framework effectively overcomes the trade-off between computational cost and hemodynamic accuracy. These findings highlight the potential of integrating CFD and machine learning as a practical clinical decision-support tool for the early prediction of thrombotic risk.

detail.abstract: This essay examines the challenges that Cuban policymakers, academics, economic actors, and civil society would face in reconstructing a legal order beyond Caribbean Marxism-Leninismunder a regime that, while not liberal democratic, is no longer tethered to the political-economic model formally adopted by the Communist Party and implemented through the State's constitutional, administrative, and operational apparatus. The analysis proceeds from a central paradox: any reconstruction undertaken while that model is being reformed or replaced must be built from the materials produced by the very system being transformed. The essay identifies the foundational problems confronting such reconstruction: the structural impossibility of "private law" under Marxist-Leninist theory, the dissolution of justice as an independent evaluative standard in both formalist and instrumentalist legal traditions, the role of scholarly communities operating under conditions of constrained intellectual autonomy, and the re-Sovietization of Cuban political-economic doctrine that has hardened rather than relaxed the orthodox framework. Drawing on comparative analysis of Chinese, Vietnamese, and post-Socialist European experiences, the essay argues that the path to legal reconstruction requires confronting-not merely replacing-the normative logic of the system from which it emerges, and that the relationship between law and politics must be rearticulated around a conception of justice that neither the pandectistic tradition nor Marxist-Leninist instrumentalism has adequately supplied. The essay ends with an action plan for reform that draws on the key insights developed in the essay to produce a six phase framework for organizing reform and "Quality Checklist" for reform proposals.

detail.abstract: Article 13(1) of Taiwan's primary competition law, the Fair Trade Act, states that the competition authorities cannot prohibit mergers if the overall economic benefit outweighs the disadvantage caused by restricted competition. However, the article is ambiguous regarding what constitutes the "overall economic benefit" and how to weigh it against the disadvantages of competition restraints. Previously treated like the total welfare standard in merger review, this article demonstrates that Taiwan is shifting toward the consumer welfare standard, in line with US antitrust law, in its interpretation of "overall economic benefit." detail.abstract: This paper studies how a reduction in public transport fares is capitalized into house prices. We develop a monocentric city model showing that public transport subsidies generate stronger housing price appreciation in peripheral locations, thereby flattening the residential bid-rent gradient. detail.abstract: We study why cash flow has become less important for investment but more important for corporate liquidity. Over time, investment-cash flow sensitivity has declined, while cash accumulation has become more sensitive to cash flow, especially among intangible-intensive firms. We embed this mechanism in a dynamic model with costly external financing and Bayesian learning. Structural estimates reproduce the joint shifts in investment and cash accumulation and imply greater reliance on non-cash-flow information. Declining investment-cash flow sensitivity therefore need not mean that internal liquidity has become less important.

detail.abstract: The post-pandemic surge in inflation led many unions and firms to alter their bargaining and wage-setting policies. Using novel German firm-level survey data, we document state dependence in wage setting across high and low inflation periods. Wage adjustment occurs along the extensive and intensive margins: the average duration of wage agreements shortens from 14.2 to 12.9 months, while adjustment per pay round increases from 2–4% to 4–6%. Newly compiled union-level panel data on collective bargaining outcomes confirm these patterns. These facts are difficult to reconcile with purely time-dependent wage-setting models but consistent with state-dependent wage setting. Using the observed wage-duration distributions, we quantify the extent to which the Generalized Wage Phillips Curve (GWPC) steepens in times of high inflation. Embedding the GWPC constructed from our firm-level and union-level data in a New Keynesian model, we find that the sacrifice ratio falls by about 13–23% in the high-inflation regime.

detail.abstract: We characterize the time-consistent solution of a cartel--fringe model of exhaustible resource extraction in which the cartel credibly acts as a von Stackelberg leader and renewable and backstop substitutes are available. For every configuration of initial resource stocks, we identify the equilibrium sequence that arises in the feedback von Stackelberg equilibrium (FBSE). We show that the FBSE exhibits three possible equilibrium extraction paths. Two of them start with a phase of simultaneous supply by the cartel and the fringe, whereas the third one starts with a phase in which the cartel is the sole supplier. We then compare the FBSE with the Nash--Cournot equilibrium (CFNE) and the open-loop von Stackelberg equilibrium (OLSE). A key distinction between the FBSE and the OLSE is that the latter never features an initial phase of simultaneous extraction, whereas such a phase emerges in the FBSE for a range of initial stock configurations. An important departure from the CFNE is that the FBSE allows for an initial phase of cartel-only supply, in which the cartel sets the price so as to keep the fringe at bay.

detail.abstract: Young people in Bayelsa State now meet the past more on their phones than in the classroom. A short TikTok video on the Biafra war, a WhatsApp broadcast on the 1914 amalgamation, or an X thread on the Benin Bronzes can reach more youths in one night than a history teacher reaches in one term. This study looked at how social media is shaping the way young people in Bayelsa State understand their history, and what this means for history education. A descriptive survey was carried out among 300 respondents aged 15 to 25, made up of 150 senior secondary school students and 150 university undergraduates in Bayelsa State. The findings show that social media is now the most frequent source of historical information (46%), led by TikTok and YouTube; that most respondents find videos easier to follow than textbooks; and that only about one in four often checks a historical claim before believing or sharing it. The study also found that social media has made many young people curious about the past, especially topics left out of the classroom or handled thinly there. The paper argues that history teachers should not fight social media but should use it, while teaching students how to question what they see. It recommends a revised curriculum with digital source evaluation, teacher training, partnership with Nigerian historians and content creators, and a stronger role for libraries, museums and archives.

detail.abstract: Patent examination of multi-component compositions and formulations under the Indian Patents Act, 1970 is plagued by a fundamental structural error: the judicial and administrative mutation of Section 3(e) from an objective, negative subject-matter eligibility filter into an improper, heightened secondary 'inventive step' requirement. By demanding that an applicant prove 'unexpected synergy,' 'surprising technical effects,' or 'unpredictability over cited prior art' to overcome a Section 3(e) objection, the Indian Patent Office (IPO) and High Courts (e.g., Novozymes, Biomoneta, Boehringer Ingelheim, Intra-Cellular Therapies, and La Roche) have collapsed Level 2 (subject-matter eligibility) into Level 3 (substantive patentability under Section 2(1)(ja)). This paper proves that Section 3(e) contains no statutory reference to 'prior art,' 'person skilled in the art (POSITA),' or 'unpredictability.' Using strict grammatical parsing, the paper demonstrates that Section 3(e) employs the restrictive adverb 'only in the aggregation of properties.' Consequently, any non-additive interaction between components-whether synergistic (1+1 > 2) OR antagonistic (1+1 < 2, such as reduced toxicity, mutual quenching, desensitization, or altered dissolution kinetics)-shatters the linear sum and clears Section 3(e) as a matter of law. Whether that non-additive interaction was predictable or obvious over prior art is an extrinsic inquiry reserved exclusively for Section 2(1)(ja). Conflating the two violates the canon against statutory surplusage, rendering Section 2(1)(ja) redundant for composition claims. Anchored in the 'Three Levels of Invention' taxonomy and comparing USPTO (35 U.S.C. § § 101/103) and EPO (Arts. 52/56 EPC) architectures, this study presents a two-stage examination blueprint to restore doctrinal discipline to Indian patent practice.

detail.abstract: The Gospel of John presents authority and agency through a complex relationship between divine commissioning and human representation. Jesus repeatedly identifies the Father as the source of his mission, authority, teaching, and works, while his followers are also commissioned to continue the mission entrusted to him. This pattern creates a framework in which divine authority is communicated through appointed representatives. Jewish concepts of agency provide an important background for understanding this relationship, particularly the principle that an authorized representative acts on behalf of the one who commissions him.
