detail.abstract: We study how a digital platform designs intertemporal commission schemes to incentivize service providers to exert quality-improvement effort, and how pricing authority and ancillary benefits shape commission design and value allocation. In the absence of ancillary benefits, the platform offers a downward-adjusting commission to service providers with intermediate effort costs, while using upward-adjusting commissions for those with either low or high effort costs. Platform-controlled pricing (PCP) and agent-controlled pricing (ACP) yield identical equilibrium outcomes in this setting. The presence of ancillary benefits changes how pricing authority affects commission design. Under PCP, ancillary benefits strengthen the service provider's private incentive to exert effort and alter the commission required to induce quality improvement. Under ACP, ancillary benefits additionally induce the service provider to underprice in order to expand adoption. Anticipating this distortion, the platform concedes a larger future revenue share, making intertemporal commission not only an effort-incentive instrument but also a second-best pricing-correction instrument; when ancillary benefits are sufficiently large, the platform may optimally waive its second-period commission. Finally, ancillary benefits increase both parties' profits under PCP but can reduce the platform's profit under ACP. Consequently, the platform prefers PCP whereas the service provider prefers ACP, revealing a conflict over pricing control arising from asymmetric revenue structures.

detail.abstract: This paper seeks to locate competition law and consumer protection in Kenya's 2010 Constitution. The Constitution names consumer rights in article 46. It never names competition law. detail.abstract: Data contracts-explicit, enforced agreements between data producers and consumers governing schema structure, data quality, and change management-have increasingly been proposed as a discipline for streaming data platforms, and Confluent Schema Registry, an open-source project with a fully published implementation, provides one of the most concretely implemented, publicly documented realizations of this concept in production use. This paper examines that implementation using Confluent's own official documentation and its open-source repository, distinguishing Schema Registry's foundational compatibility-type enforcement, available since early versions of the product, from its more recently formalized "Data Contracts" feature, which requires Confluent Platform version 7.4 or above and either Confluent Enterprise licensing or Confluent Cloud's Advanced Stream Governance package. We document all seven officially defined compatibility types-BACKWARD, BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE, FORWARD, FORWARD_TRANSITIVE, FULL, FULL_TRANSITIVE, and NONE-and Confluent's own stated rationale for BACKWARD as the default, that it allows consumers to be rewound to the beginning of a topic and still read historical data correctly. We examine the Data Contracts feature's three components-tags, metadata, and rules, the latter expressed as CEL or JSONata expressions supporting both data-quality validation and schema-version migration-and document a specific, officially stated enforcement gap directly relevant to production deployment: rule execution is explicitly not supported by Kafka Connect on Confluent Cloud, by Flink SQL, or by ksqlDB on either platform, and applies only to a schema's root definition rather than any referenced sub-schemas. detail.abstract: "We quantify the short-term impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) on sales performance through a series of large-scale randomized field experiments involving millions of users and products at a leading cross-border online retail platform. Over 2023-2024, the platform integrated GenAI into seven business workflows spanning customer service, consumer-product matching, advertising, and seller services. We find that GenAI adoption increases sales in most workflows, with effects ranging from no detectable impact to 16.3%, depending on GenAI’s marginal contribution relative to baseline firm practices. Across the four GenAI applications with positive sales effects, the implied annual incremental value is roughly $5 per consumer—an economically meaningful impact given the retailer’s scale and the early stage of GenAI adoption. The gains operate primarily through higher conversion rates rather than larger cart values, consistent with GenAI improving the shopping experience by reducing search, information, communication, and personalization frictions. Importantly, these effects are not associated with worse post-purchase outcomes, as product return rates and customer ratings do not deteriorate. Finally, we document substantial demand-side heterogeneity, with larger gains for less experienced consumers. Our findings provide novel, large-scale causal evidence on how GenAI shapes sales productivity in online retail, highlighting both its immediate value and broader potential."

detail.abstract: We exploit the sharp escalation in community-based interior immigration enforcement following the January 2025 inauguration to estimate its effect on aggregate consumer spending. Using Synthetic Difference-in-Differences, we compare states experiencing relatively large increases in community-based enforcement with states experiencing smaller increases. States exposed to larger enforcement surges experienced aggregate card spending declines of approximately 1.7 percentage points relative to their synthetic controls, an effect robust to alternative specifications and sample definitions. A parallel treatment constructed from jail-based arrests, a less visible form of enforcement, produces statistically null estimates, while non-in-person spending is similarly unaffected. Together, these contrasts are consistent with enforcement visibility playing an important role in shaping consumer spending responses. Sectoral estimates reveal substantial heterogeneity across political environments: spending declines in Democratic-governed states are concentrated in restaurants and other in-person activities, while declines in Trump-voting states are concentrated in sectors such as home improvement and transportation and warehousing. By focusing on aggregate spending responses rather than the immediate effects of individual enforcement operations, our analysis complements recent studies of localized enforcement events by estimating the cumulative state-level consumer spending consequences of differential exposure to community-based immigration enforcement across sectors and political environments.

detail.abstract: We study the impact of soil endowments on children's health outcomes in India. Using nationally representative cross section data, we find that a transition from fully clayey to fully loamy soil reduces the probability of stunting, wasting and underweight of children under 5 years by 2.3, 3.6 and 4.7 percentage points respectively. Reduced female labor force participation in loamy regions mitigates backlash effect from the household, leading to lower intimate partner violence, thereby acting as a plausible channel to explain our findings.

detail.abstract: The internationalization of major Chinese online travel platforms (OTAs) across South Asia represents a fundamental transition from standard transactional booking distribution to collaborative platform-to-business (P2B) ecosystems. Grounded in Service-Dominant (S-D) Logic and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, this study develops a conceptual framework examining P2B value co-creation between Chinese digital platforms and independent accommodation providers in Bangladesh. Authored from the operational perspective of an active Bangladeshi hotelier, the paper analyzes value co-creation across three key dimensions: bidirectional operational data exchange, technological infrastructure synchronization, and localized cross-cultural service delivery. The review examines the empirical realities of Bangladeshi hoteliers—who routinely bridge digital infrastructure gaps to service Chinese business delegations—and addresses structural frictions, power asymmetries, and revenue yield optimization. Finally, it establishes an actionable multi-case research agenda designed for emerging-market practitioners and management scholars along the Digital Silk Road.

detail.abstract: How does access to physical space shape scientific productivity? We study the staggered reopening of Chinese university campuses after the COVID-19 pandemic. We hand-collect campus reopening dates and access regimes and link them to 7.32 million OpenAlex publications from 2010 to 2025. Using universities that remained closed or required reservations as comparison groups, our differencein-differences estimates show that full reopening increases both the quantity and the quality of scientific output. Reopening expands collaboration with other universities and firms and facilitates new research ties, consistent with lower search and matching costs. The effects are larger at universities with stronger basicresearch capacity, more laboratory facilities, and greater disciplinary diversity, consistent with lower project execution costs in research environments that depend more heavily on physical interaction. The gains are concentrated in engineering, agricultural sciences, and economics and management, fields in which face-to-face interaction or access to experimental facilities is especially relevant. The results show that campus accessibility is an important institutional condition linking physical proximity to scientific collaboration and knowledge production.

detail.abstract: An institution must choose both a cooperative allocation and which coalition technologies to verify. We study this joint decision in a nontransferable-utility burdensharing game with costly local audits. Some coalitions may possess an unknown bypass technology, and a deviation requires every member to gain strictly. For any efficient allocation, we characterize the exact information certificate needed for robust implementation: with heterogeneous service caps, audit costs, and technologically possible coalitions, the institution must clear precisely the possible bypass coalitions contained in the set of participants below their caps. The allocation therefore creates its own information requirement. The certificate is exponential when arbitrarily large coalitions may possess bypasses, but polynomial when bypass size is bounded. Under a symmetric single-exception prior, we solve the unrestricted adaptive acquisitionallocation problem and show that higher audit costs narrow the optimal burden-sharing group. Multiple exceptions create inference across coalition technologies. Finally, weakening strict consent, directly or through side payments that compensate otherwise indifferent members, can sharply increase the information needed to construct stability.

detail.abstract: Institutions can control who may cooperate even when they cannot freely rewrite how cooperative surplus is shared. We study a transferable-utility communication game in which a designer pays to enable bilateral cooperation rights, surplus is allocated by the Myerson value, and members join only if payoffs meet known participation requirements. Connectivity fixes grand-coalition production, but architecture changes its distribution. For convex games, we characterize the maximum payoff a player can obtain while remaining a leaf; the resulting peripheral-payoff frontier converts participation into topological restrictions and can rule out every tree. Heterogeneous link costs then price the organizational positions needed for retention. These implementation costs can make it efficient to exclude a participant who contributes positive net productive surplus. With bounded pledgeable side payments, rights and contracts become substitute instruments, and optimal architecture and membership change at contractibility thresholds. Thus costly cooperation rights matter even after productive connectivity is achieved.

detail.abstract: Compliance with summit commitments is the main evidence on whether the BRICS keeps its word, and the figure that summarises it, 77 per cent average compliance, is computed on the small subset of commitments that an external monitor chooses to assess. This monograph examines that choice. It builds the first commitment-level dataset of the 18 BRICS leaders' declarations of 2009–2026 (1,714 candidate commitments) and links it to the 14 final compliance reports of the BRICS Research Group for 2011–2024. The monitor's own counts of the universe of commitments are unstable across its publications. Coverage is structurally low, 5–18 per cent of commitments per summit, with no trend over time, and falls as declarations grow longer. Selection favours strongly worded commitments and, less robustly, pledges of money. Selection on observable attributes does not bias reported compliance (69.8 per cent reported, 70.1 per cent corrected), but assumption-free bounds span 7.2 to 97.1 per cent, and a correlation of only 0.15 between selection and compliance would shift the published figure by 10 points. The figure is accurate about what it measures, but it measures little. Volume VII of The Gap Series. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23107090.
